title: new and delete
concept: new allocates memory on the heap, and delete frees it.

steps.title: Allocating memory on the heap
steps.explanation:
`new int(42)` allocates space of size int on the heap and initializes it to 42.

The returned address is stored in pointer `p`. This is a structure where `p` on the stack points to data on the heap.

steps.title: Dereference and print
steps.explanation: Read the value 42 stored in the heap with `*p`.

steps.title: Release with delete
steps.explanation:
`delete p` returns heap memory to the operating system.

**Note**: After delete, `p` still contains the old address (dangling pointer). To prevent this, initialize it with `p = nullptr`.

quiz.question: Why do I set the pointer to nullptr after delete?
quiz.explanation: After delete, the pointer becomes a dangling pointer pointing to freed memory. Setting it to nullptr will cause an immediate crash when accidentally accessed, making debugging easier.

misconceptions.wrong: When you call delete, the pointer automatically becomes nullptr.
misconceptions.correct: delete only releases heap memory and does not change the value of the pointer variable.
misconceptions.why: In C++, a pointer is a simple address value, so the programmer must manually set it to nullptr.

keyTakeaway: new/delete is the basis for manual memory management, but it's easy to forget, so smart pointers are safer.
